GROWTH-TO-STANDARD USING GEORGIA MILESTONES

 Damian W Betebenner
 National Center for the Improvement of Educational Assessment
 Atlanta, Georgia February 27th, 2018

BACKGROUND
• Since their development, SGP analyses have supported both norm- and
 criterion-referenced student growth analyses.

• Norm-referenced results are more prominently used than the
 criterion-referenced analyses, particularly with respect to accountability.

• Criterion-referenced SGP analyses were submitted and approved as
 part of the Growth Model Pilot Program under Secretary Spellings
 during the Bush Administration.

• There is renewed interest in looking at growth-to standard with ESSA
 for state summative and ELP assessment with several states using
 growth-to-standard as part of their accountability plans.

BACKGROUND
• The norm- and criterion-referenced component of SGP analyses are
 the SGP (student growth percentile) and the AGP (adequate growth
 percentile).

• AGP calculation requires establishing an ending achievement target
 and a time frame to reach the target.

• The most common achievement goal is proficiency/career & college
 readiness.

• The most common time frame is 3 years.

• As part of AGP calculation, AGPs are calculated for all possible time
 frames (1, 2, …) and all possible achievement level cutscores.

STUDENT GROWTH PERCENTILES/
PROJECTIONS
• SGP analyses produce coefficient matrices for each of 100 quantile values:
 .005, .015, .025, .035, …, .975, .985, .995

• Using these matrices, 100 quantile cuts are established for each student based upon
 their scale score history (independent variables) and used to associate a student’s scale
 score (dependent variable) with an integer from 0 to 100 (inclusive). 0s and 100s are
 usually converted to 1s and 99s.

• The coefficient matrices allow for the calculation of 100 percentile growth trajectories
 for a student: Student Growth Projections

• AGPs (Adequate Growth Percentiles) are determined by examining the 100 trajectories
 and finding the minimal trajectory that allows the student to reach the desired
 destination in the given time-frame.

• AGP are like scale-score trajectories but they smooth “difficulty” (equal percentile
 growth for the duration of the trajectory).

STUDENT GROWTH PERCENTILES/
PROJECTIONS: DETAILS
• For example, consider how we construct 100 percentile trajectories for a 3rd Grade student starting at the
 Beginning/Developing ELA cutscore of 475:

 • Step 1: To derive 100 grade 4 projections we use the grade 3 to grade 4 coefficient matrix with a grade
 3 scaled score of 475.

 • Step 2: To derive the 100 grade 5 projections we use the grade 3/4 to grade 5 coefficient matrix with
 the grade 3 scaled score of 475 and the 100 grade 4 projections from step 1.

 • Step 3: To derive the 100 grade 6 projections we use the grade 4/5 to grade 6 coefficient matrix with
 the 100 grade 4 projections and 100 grade 5 projections.

 • Step 4: To derive the 100 grade 7 projections we use the grade 5/6 to grade 7 coefficient matrix with
 the 100 grade 5 projections and 100 grade 6 projections.

 • Step 5: To derive the 100 grade 8 projections we use the grade 6/7 to grade 8 coefficient matrix with
 the 100 grade 6 projections and 100 grade 7 projections.

 • Step 6: To derive the 100 grade 9 Lit projections we use the Grade 7/8 to grade 9 lit coefficient matrix
 with the 100 grade 7 projections and the 100 grade 8 projections.

 • Step 7: To derive the 100 american lit projections we use the Grade 8/9 lit to American lit coefficient
 matrix with the 100 grade 8 projections and the 100 grade 9 lit projections.

FROM PROJECTIONS TO AN AGP

• Percentile trajectories (projections) need to be converted to a single
 target based upon a time frame and an achievement goal.

• Most states use a 3 year time frame to proficiency. Georgia is
 considering a 3 year time frame to each of the top 3 achievement
 levels (3 cutscores).

WHAT DOES “ON TRACK” MEAN

• Common parlance is often used to try and put a sophisticated idea into “layman’s
 terms”. “On track to reach proficiency” or “On track to catch-up to proficiency”
 are two common phrases in this regard.

• There is general confusion about what the term “on track” means (e.g., the student
 is “on track to reach proficiency”). E.g., “The student will reach proficiency.”

• My Take: “On Track” has one of two meanings depending upon whether a pre-
 specified “pathway to proficiency” plan is established:

 • No plan: Assuming “typical” rates of progress continue, the student will reach
 proficiency.

 • Yes plan: The student is hitting interim targets and assuming they continue to hit
 these targets will reach proficiency.

ON TRACK

• A student is considered to be "on track" if their SGP >= AGP (that is,
 they grew more than their target).

• An AGP can be converted to a sequence of 1, 2, 3, … Tmax scale
 scores such that the student can compare their scale score to a target
 scale score to determine whether they are "on track”

• The scale score trajectory will be curvi-linear such that each segment
 has the same “difficulty”. This differs from a linear scale score
 trajectory.

ANOMALIES

• In a very few cases (generally < 1%) a student will not reach their
 achievement goal but their AGP >= SGP

• This situation occurs when consecutive quantile cuts encompass both
 the cutscore as well as an adjacent cut.

• For example, a student scores 474 on the Grade 5 ELA. Their score is
 in the (.415, .425] quantile interval (473.2, 475] and receives an SGP of
 42. Their 1-year AGP is also 42 (since both 474 and 475 are in that
 interval). They hit their 1-year catch-up target but didn’t catch-up.

• If AGP are converted to scaled score targets, this situation can be
 avoided

OTHER CONSIDERATIONS

• Georgia currently uses/reports measurement error corrected
 (SIMEX) SGPs, projections are calculated using observed score
 coefficient matrices.

• This is justified (and preferred) because (Carroll, 2009):

 • “… if future observation of X are also measured with an error then
 it is rarely necessary to address the measurement error as
 prediction of Y can be achieved via estimate by standard non-
 parametric regression estimators from the sample.”

BIBLIOGRAPHY

• Carroll, R. J., Delaigle, A., & Hall, P., Nonparametric prediction in
 measurement error models. J Am Stat Association. 2009 Sep 1;
 104(487): 993-1014

LAGGED VERSUS CURRENT PROJECTIONS
• Two types of projections are calculated: Lagged and Current projections.

• Lagged projections provide the AGP targets used for growth-to-
 standard.

• Lagged projections apply the most recent coefficient matrices (those
 use to produce the student’s current SGP) to calculate a target. Thus
 SGP and AGP are based upon the same norms.

• Current projections are used to provide forward looking targets.

• When baseline analyses are used, lagged targets and current targets
 don’t change. Annual re-norming can cause some discrepancies between
 current and lagged targets.

TIME FRAME TO REACH GOAL
• Times frames used for growth-to-standard can either be fixed in time
 or fixed in duration (“rolled forward”).

• Fixed time frames mandate the student reach proficiency at a
 particular time/grade.

• Fixed in duration time frames (e.g., 3 years) are usually extended each
 year to yield new targets.

• AGP calculations can support either approach to setting a time-frame.

• Fixed in time approaches usually yield a “balloon payment” for students
 who have failed to make intermediate targets. This causes problems for
 accountability systems.
